Marketing and sourcing03 / 04

From a first taste to a repeat order

General marketing plan

01

Education through short videos

Show the farm, flavour and a simple brew on Reels and TikTok. Publish the roast date and tasting notes for each lot.

02

Tastings and trusted creators

Offer creator samples and community tastings in Singapore. Collect feedback and track sales through unique links.

03

A clear offer at checkout

Use one landing page with the delivered price and recipe. Add referral rewards. Test paid ads after the first sales.

04

Support that earns reorders

Help buyers brew their first bag. Send opt-in reorder reminders and offer new lots. Add subscriptions after repeat sales.

Pilot milestone: 15 paid orders. Measure CAC, conversion and 30-day reorders. Budget RM8/order for acquisition, including samples and rewards.

Sources and model notes

Updated 5 October 2026. The four-slide deck follows the supplied “Sunway X Teleport .pdf”: product, target customer, marketing and unit economics. All source numbers are clickable. The HTML uses the fixed 1920 × 1080 stage from Zara Zhang’s Frontend Slides, with navigation and inline editing. This revision describes Malaysian Liberica as the venture's product and keeps suppliers as options.

1. Arabica pressure and Malaysian production

Grüter et al. (2022) model Arabica suitability in 2050 under three climate pathways. Highly suitable growing area falls by more than 50% in all three scenarios. This is a projection of land suitability, not a forecast that actual production falls by 50%. USDA's July 2026 table reports global Arabica output of 102.276m 60 kg bags in 2024/25, 94.440m in 2025/26, and 105.867m forecast in 2026/27. Calculated changes are −7.66% and +12.10%. These data support recent supply pressure and a rebound, rather than a steady long-run production decline. Crop cycles and weather matter.

Bernama's 3 December 2025 report attributes the Malaysian cultivation figures to Agriculture and Food Security Minister Mohamad Sabu's parliamentary response. Liberica represents 87% of cultivation, with Robusta 10% and Arabica 3%. The total 2024 coffee cultivation area is 2,924 ha and all-variety output is 2,861 metric tonnes. The 2,924 ha figure must not be presented as Liberica-only area. Domestic growing capability supports sourcing, but does not establish uncommitted export supply.

The launch model purchases roasted coffee from established Malaysian growers/roasters and uses a suitable packing partner. New planting is a later option with grower partners after repeat demand. Its land, planting, maturation, processing, capital and operating costs are outside this purchase-and-resell order model. The venture should obtain a separate farm plan before claiming farm profitability. Supplier product photography illustrates an existing Malaysian product, not the venture's final brand or a signed agreement.

2. Singapore demand and persona

YouGov's July 2024 survey covers 1,064 Singapore residents and weights the sample to Singapore adults aged 18+. It reports 58% drinking coffee daily. The 31% who brewed at home more are specifically consumers reporting higher prices for their usual coffee purchases. That percentage is not 31% of all residents. Both findings describe coffee overall, including formats beyond specialty whole beans.

WITS / UN Comtrade reports Singapore's 2024 gross imports under HS 090121 (roasted coffee, not decaffeinated) at 4,924,690 kg and US$68,478,380. Malaysia supplies 2,421,550 kg and US$16,554,570. The computed Malaysian share is 49.17% by weight. Gross imports can include re-exports, capsules and different coffee species. These figures are evidence of an established roasted-coffee trade and must not be labelled Singapore's domestic consumption or Liberica market size.

MORNING's Singapore listing offers 10 Liberica capsules for S$22, from its Singapore warehouse. This is direct evidence of local retail adoption of Malaysian Liberica in a different format. The retailer does not disclose sales volume here. Do not infer whole-bean volume, sell-through, total addressable Liberica demand or exclusivity from the listing. The persona “Jia, 30”, occupation, equipment, budget, monthly quantity and behaviour are design hypotheses. Interview home brewers and validate with paid orders.

3. Supplier options and average price

MCR offers Liberica from its Pahang plantation and private-label formats. Its published OEM timeline is typically 6–10 weeks. No verified public Liberica price or agreed MOQ was found, so no MCR price is included in the average. Obtain an actual quotation and confirm roast, processing, pack format, traceability and Singapore distributors. Libta, MY LIBERICA and House of Kendal offer alternative Malaysian sourcing options. Several Malaysian suppliers already ship to Singapore. The pitch competes through its chosen lot and customer service rather than assuming Singapore has no access.

The unit model uses the simple, unweighted mean of two observed 1 kg roasted Liberica pack prices: Libta 1 KG at RM137 and MY LIBERICA Jackfruit 1 kg at RM168. Average = (137 + 168) / 2 = RM152.50/kg. These are posted retail purchasing benchmarks before any shipping, wholesale discount or private-label fee. The two coffees differ in roast and processing, so the result is a planning sample average, not a market-wide statistical average or a supplier quotation. The slide's supplier links allow price checking.

Libta's size selector / product data confirms 250 G RM45, 500 G RM87 and 1 KG RM137 (variant 32156655517792). MY LIBERICA's product-variation data confirms 200 g RM56 and 1 kg RM168. House of Kendal's Bagan Ningrat is RM60/250 g. Its smaller pack is not mixed into the 1 kg sample average. For price sensitivity only, the earlier four small-pack benchmarks normalize to RM120, RM180, RM240 and RM280/kg, averaging RM205/kg. They represent a different pack-size basis.

4. Marketing plan and measurement

The general plan uses short-form education, authentic creator sampling, community tastings, a clear delivered-price checkout and replenishment reminders with customer opt-in. Focus on a batch-specific flavour and practical recipe. Content and marketing costs include samples, packing, sample shipping, creator fees, referral rewards and any advertising. All paid creator costs should enter measured acquisition cost. First aim for 15 paid orders and use conversion, acquisition cost and 30-day reorder behaviour to decide whether to expand stock. No channel response or sales volume is guaranteed.

The RM8 marketing allocation is a planning target for variable acquisition cost per order, not a verified Singapore advertising rate. General marketing replaces the previous detailed 14-day campaign. Actual CAC = relevant acquisition spend / new paid customers. Founder time and continuing overhead remain fixed business costs. Do not increase advertising based only on views or sample requests.

5. Economics and assumptions

One sales unit is 400 g in two 200 g bags, delivered to one Singapore customer in one parcel. Proposed selling price is S$49.90. The model retains RM3.1878 per SGD from the earlier BNM reference check on 5 October 2026 as a fixed model rate. It is not a promise of the payment processor's settlement rate. Gross receipts = 49.90 × 3.1878 = RM159.07122, rounded RM159.07. Update the conversion assumption when quoting or launching.

Beans = 0.400 kg / 98% packing yield × RM152.50/kg = RM62.24489796, rounded RM62.24. COGS = RM62.24 + RM3 packaging + RM2 packing labour = RM67.24. The 2% handling loss is assumed. A partner must quote suitable repacking or supplier-filled 200 g bags. Posted 1 kg pricing does not guarantee that supplier-filled 200 g private-label packs cost the same per kilogram. If smaller supplier packs are required, recalculate COGS.

Payment costs assume a Malaysia Stripe merchant charging SGD and settling MYR: 3% online card rate + 1% international card + 2% currency conversion + RM1 per charge. Cost = 6% × RM159.07 + RM1 = RM10.54 rounded. Payment Links is included, so incremental platform fee is RM0. The model includes currency conversion once. Add any separately quoted storefront or marketplace cost if the sales channel changes.

The source Teleport brief page 6 gives an indicative RM20 for the first 1 kg MY-to-SG parcel. This is a classroom assumption, not a live TNX quote. The model charges the full parcel minimum rather than prorating by 400 g of beans. Actual packed and volumetric weights must qualify. It assumes doorstep delivery without SG warehousing or another delivery leg. RM5 is an unquoted service/clearance allowance. Final carrier scope and importer costs need confirmation.

Tax contingency = 9% of gross receipts = RM14.32 and returns/spoilage reserve = 2% = RM3.18. The tax contingency is a conservative budget, not a calculation of payable GST. Actual import GST or overseas-vendor obligations depend on shipment method, importer status, CIF value and relevant low-value rules. The brief reserve should be reconciled to actual tax rather than represented as statutory assessment. Use the appropriate Singapore commercial-food-import registration and permit route.

Total variable costs and reserves = RM128.28. Contribution = RM159.07 − RM128.28 = RM30.79, or 19.4%. It excludes fixed startup and compliance setup, salaries, income tax and farm investment. Shipping at RM30 reduces contribution to RM20.79. Beans at RM205/kg after 2% handling loss cost RM83.67, reducing contribution to RM9.36. Approximate order break-even price is S$38.26 under the same model before fixed business costs. Averages do not guarantee an actual achievable purchase price.

Fifteen 400 g orders require 6.0 kg net coffee or about 6.122 kg before handling loss, plus marketing samples. Seven 1 kg bags at the sample average would cost RM1,067.50 as an illustrative stock budget. The actual invoice will depend on supplier choice and pack quantity. Remaining coffee is inventory. Initial cash outlay is not the same as consumed per-order COGS.
